prompt: In the BDFL model as practiced by Redis under Salvatore Sanfilippo (antirez) through 2020, how did a contested design decision (such as whether to add multithreading) actually get resolved?
choices: antirez made the final call himself after weighing the tradeoffs, with no formal vote required
A PMC vote was held requiring three binding +1 votes
The decision was put to a community-wide GitHub poll
A dedicated SIG reviewed a KEP-style proposal before approval

prompt: Under the ASF's governance model as practiced by Apache Kafka's PMC, what does 'lazy consensus' mean in practice?
choices: A change is treated as approved if nobody with standing objects within a defined time window, with no explicit vote cast at all
Every change, no matter how small, requires at least three binding +1 votes
The project's original author retains a permanent veto on all future changes
Lazy consensus applies only to release votes, never to ordinary code changes

prompt: Kafka's KIP-500 proposed replacing ZooKeeper with a self-managed metadata quorum (KRaft). What actually happened to the proposal between being filed in 2019 and the feature being marked production-ready in Kafka 3.3 (2022)?
choices: It was split into follow-on proposals (covering the Raft protocol and the controller architecture separately) and rolled out through a multi-year bridge period rather than shipping as one atomic change
It was rejected by the PMC on the first vote and never revisited
It shipped completely unchanged, exactly as originally proposed, within the same release cycle
It bypassed the KIP process entirely because it was classified as an internal refactor

prompt: In the Tier 3 RFC template (the RFC-014 structure), what is the specific purpose of the 'Alternatives considered' section?
choices: To show reviewers which other options were evaluated and why they were rejected, so the choice isn't re-litigated later
To list every possible future extension of the current proposal
To record the author's personal opinion of competing open-source projects
To satisfy a CI linter that checks the document for a minimum word count

prompt: A maintainer's review comment explains the underlying cause of a bug, points to precedent elsewhere in the codebase, and asks the contributor to add a regression test -- instead of just saying 'fix the Kind check.' What does this demonstrate?
choices: It teaches the contributor transferable knowledge about the codebase, rather than only correcting this one line
It shows that maintainers should always rewrite a contributor's code themselves instead of asking questions
It proves that first-time contributors should be held to a lower bar than experienced ones
It demonstrates that the maintainer fundamentally disagrees with the contributor's entire approach

prompt: How does a binding -1 veto function in the ASF voting model, compared to a BDFL's unilateral 'no'?
choices: An ASF binding -1 must come with a technical justification and forces further discussion or revision, rather than being automatically final the way a BDFL's decision can be
Both function identically -- a single person's objection ends the proposal permanently either way
A BDFL's 'no' legally requires a 72-hour public comment period before it takes effect
An ASF -1 vote is non-binding and the proposer is free to ignore it and merge anyway

prompt: Why does reusing Tier 3's RFC-014 section structure (Context, Problem, Alternatives, Tradeoffs, Rollout plan, Open questions) still work for a proposal as large as Kafka's KIP-500?
choices: The sections scale with the size of the content inside them, not with the format itself -- the discipline of writing each section is what matters, regardless of the proposal's scope
Because the ASF legally requires every project to use that exact template
Because KIP-500 was, as a matter of historical fact, originally written in that literal file
Because reviewers refuse to read any RFC format they have not seen before

prompt: In the ASF's three-tier structure (contributor, committer, PMC member), what specifically changes as someone moves up a tier?
choices: They gain binding authority -- their votes count toward the thresholds required to approve code changes, releases, and new committers
They begin receiving a dedicated salary directly from the foundation
They lose the ability to submit pull requests directly to the project
They are automatically appointed BDFL of a new sub-project
